title: From Financial Autonomy to Local Accountability: Implementing Local Government Autonomy in Gombe State, Nigeria
content: Local-government autonomy is intended to strengthen subnational discretion over public resources, but greater financial access does not necessarily produce substantive autonomy or better budget implementation. This study examines Nigeria's 2024 local-government autonomy reform using Gombe State as a subnational case. A mixed-methods design combines financial records for all 11 LGAs in 2023–2024 with semi-structured interviews on fund control, state–LGA relations, budget implementation and accountability. Quantitative analysis uses descriptive statistics, year-on-year changes, Pearson correlations and principal component analysis across 22 LGA-year observations. Mean total revenue increased from 3,423.14 in 2023 to 5,126.46 in 2024, while actual expenditure rose from 3,085.93 to 4,716.27. However, IGR remained about 1% of total revenue, while revenue and expenditure implementation declined from 80.44% to 65.64% and from 72.55% to 59.07%, respectively. Financial responses were highly heterogeneous, particularly in IGR growth and capital expenditure. IGR share was not significantly associated with implementation, whereas revenue and expenditure implementation were strongly associated. Interviews indicate that financial access remained shaped by administrative procedures, state–LGA relations and accountability constraints. The findings show that financial expansion alone did not produce substantive autonomy, highlighting the need to align financial discretion, implementation capacity and accountability.
